newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Eurotunnel to hold debt plan vote.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Eurotunnel to hold debt plan vote.

text.p: Channel Tunnel operator Eurotunnel looked to have lined up a majority of shareholders in favour of a crucial 70 billion franc ($11.7 billion) ($11.7 billion) debt restructuring plan at an extraordinary general meeting on Thursday.
The company said executive chairman Patrick Ponsolle held proxies for 177.7 million votes representing 19.32 percent.
It said in a statement that votes for 272.3 million shares were present or represented at the meeting, or 29.62 percent of the total.
Christian Cambier of the Eurotunnel Shareholders' Association, who said before the meeting that his group would vote for the deal, holds proxies for 2.05 percent.
Belgium's Tractebel and its Belga Manche unit will vote their 10 million shares in favour of the deal, Tractebel said.

Eurotunnel needs the approval of holders of two-thirds of the French shares and three-quarters of the British shares to pursue the deal struck in April to ease the crushing debt-servicing burden on the company.
But the deal would also reduce shareholders' equity to 54.5 percent, giving Eurotunnel's creditor banks 45.5 percent.
The active shareholders' association, Adacte -- which holds some 12 million proxy votes out of the total 920 million -- was among the opponents of the debt restructuring.
Last week the French and British governments said they would consider extending Eurotunnel's operating licence to 99 years from the current 65.

They also said that if the debt deal was not approved, they would not be able to keep the banks from taking over Eurotunnel's operating licence -- a declaration that swayed shareholder rights activist Sophie l'Helias, who holds proxies for 0.8 percent.
Others who had switched in favour of the deal include Bermuda-based Northern Cross Investments.

Ponsolle told the meeting the company was on track to improve its performance. He reiterated that it expected to show a loss of 2.72 billion francs this year, less than half the 1996 loss of 6.1 billion francs.
The improvement hinges on the debt plan being approved which would lower interest charges to 3.2 billion francs for this year from 5.7 billion paid in 1996.
He said he was "extremely confident" the group could reach the targets previously set to turn a profit in 2005 and pay a dividend the following year.
Eurotunnel has been hobbled from the outset by a construction bill of 10 billion pounds, nearly twice the original cost estimate for the 51-km sub-sea link, and lower-than-targetted revenue.

The agreement struck with the banks in April followed more than a year of negotiations. Shareholders were due to vote on the plan at a meeting on June 24 that was cancelled when not enough shareholders attended. ($ = 5.959 French Francs)
